## What measures the size of a vector? {#what-measures-the-size-of-a-vector}

Coordinates describe a vector; an inner product adds geometry

- Dot products in $\reals^n$
- Weighted measurements when coordinates have different scales
- Integrals comparing functions

::: {.key-point}
Choose the inner product to match what size and similarity mean in the problem
:::


## The real inner-product axioms {#the-real-inner-product-axioms}

An inner product on a real vector space $V$ assigns $\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle\in\reals$

For all vectors and real scalars:
\begin{align*}
\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle&=\langle\vct{v},\vct{u}\rangle\\
\langle a\vct{u}+b\vct{v},\vct{w}\rangle
&=a\langle\vct{u},\vct{w}\rangle+b\langle\vct{v},\vct{w}\rangle\\
\langle\vct{v},\vct{v}\rangle&\ge0,\qquad
\langle\vct{v},\vct{v}\rangle=0\iff\vct{v}=\vct{0}
\end{align*}

Symmetry makes linearity hold in both arguments


## Weights change the geometry {#weights-change-the-geometry}

\begin{gather*}
\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle_{\mat{W}}=\vct{u}^\top\mat{W}\vct{v},\qquad
\mat{W}=\mat{W}^\top\text{ positive definite}\\
\mat{W}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&4\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\left\|\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{bmatrix}\right\|_{\mat{W}}^2=x_1^2+4x_2^2
\end{gather*}

The weighted unit circle is an ellipse in standard coordinates

For $\vct{u}=[1,1]^\top$ and $\vct{v}=[4,-1]^\top$:
$\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle_{\mat{W}}=0$ but $\vct{u}^\top\vct{v}=3$

---

### Check the weighted inner-product axioms {#check-the-weighted-inner-product-axioms}

For symmetric positive-definite $\mat{W}$:
\begin{align*}
\langle\vct{v},\vct{u}\rangle_{\mat{W}}
&=(\vct{v}^\top\mat{W}\vct{u})^\top
=\vct{u}^\top\mat{W}^\top\vct{v}
=\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle_{\mat{W}}\\
\langle a\vct{u}+b\vct{v},\vct{w}\rangle_{\mat{W}}
&=a\vct{u}^\top\mat{W}\vct{w}+b\vct{v}^\top\mat{W}\vct{w}\\
\langle\vct{v},\vct{v}\rangle_{\mat{W}}
&=\vct{v}^\top\mat{W}\vct{v}>0\quad(\vct{v}\ne\vct{0})
\end{align*}

In the example: $1\cdot4+4\cdot1\cdot(-1)=0$

The same vectors need not be perpendicular under two different inner products


## Continuous functions also have geometry {#continuous-functions-also-have-geometry}

On $C([0,1])$, define
\begin{equation*}
\langle f,g\rangle=\int_0^1 f(t)g(t)\,\dif t
\end{equation*}

- Symmetry and linearity come from the integral
- A nonzero continuous function has a positive integral of its square
- Similarity compares entire functions, not only their sampled values

For $f(t)=1$, $g(t)=t$: $\langle f,g\rangle=1/2$

::: {.notes}
Continuity guarantees positive definiteness for actual functions. For general square-integrable functions, use equivalence classes modulo equality almost everywhere to obtain an inner-product space. Completeness and Hilbert spaces are later-course context.
:::

---

### Why a zero integral forces a continuous function to vanish {#continuous-function-positive-definiteness}

Suppose $f$ is continuous and $f(t_0)\ne0$ at some $t_0\in[0,1]$

Continuity supplies an interval $J\subseteq[0,1]$ of positive length with
\begin{gather*}
|f(t)|\ge\frac{|f(t_0)|}{2}\quad(t\in J)\\
\int_0^1f(t)^2\,\dif t
\ge\int_Jf(t)^2\,\dif t
\ge\frac{|f(t_0)|^2}{4}\operatorname{length}(J)>0
\end{gather*}

Therefore $\langle f,f\rangle=0$ only for the zero continuous function

The integral adds squared values; positive and negative values cannot cancel


## Norms, distances, and angles follow {#norms-distances-and-angles-follow}

\begin{gather*}
\|\vct{v}\|=\sqrt{\langle\vct{v},\vct{v}\rangle},\qquad
d(\vct{u},\vct{v})=\|\vct{u}-\vct{v}\|\\
\cos\theta=\frac{\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle}{\|\vct{u}\|\|\vct{v}\|},
\quad\vct{u},\vct{v}\ne\vct{0}
\end{gather*}

Cauchy–Schwarz: $|\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle|\le\|\vct{u}\|\|\vct{v}\|$

Triangle inequality: $\|\vct{u}+\vct{v}\|\le\|\vct{u}\|+\|\vct{v}\|$

::: {.notes}
Cauchy–Schwarz follows by minimizing ||u-tv||^2 over real t when v is nonzero. Equality occurs exactly for linearly dependent vectors. Expand the squared norm and apply the inequality to obtain the triangle inequality.
:::

---

### The angle between the functions $1$ and $t$ {#angle-between-one-and-t}

On $[0,1]$, let $f(t)=1$, $g(t)=t$, and $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_0^1f(t)g(t)\,\dif t$
\begin{align*}
\langle f,g\rangle&=\int_0^1t\,\dif t=\left[\frac{t^2}{2}\right]_0^1=\frac12\\
\|f\|_{L^2}&=\left(\int_0^1 1^2\,\dif t\right)^{1/2}=1\\
\|g\|_{L^2}&=\left(\int_0^1t^2\,\dif t\right)^{1/2}
=\sqrt{\left[\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^1}=\frac1{\sqrt3}\\
\cos\theta&=\frac{\langle f,g\rangle}{\|f\|_{L^2}\|g\|_{L^2}}
=\frac{1/2}{1\cdot(1/\sqrt3)}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
$\theta=\arccos(\sqrt3/2)=\pi/6=30^\circ$ — the angle between functions, not their plotted graphs
:::

---

### Derive Cauchy–Schwarz from a nonnegative square {#derive-cauchy-schwarz}

For $\vct{v}\ne\vct{0}$, choose $c=\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle/\|\vct{v}\|^2$
\begin{align*}
0\le\|\vct{u}-c\vct{v}\|^2
&=\|\vct{u}\|^2-2c\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle+c^2\|\vct{v}\|^2\\
&=\|\vct{u}\|^2-\frac{\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle^2}{\|\vct{v}\|^2}\\
\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle^2
&\le\|\vct{u}\|^2\|\vct{v}\|^2
\end{align*}

Take square roots; if $\vct{v}=\vct{0}$, both sides are zero

Equality holds exactly when the two vectors are linearly dependent

---

### Derive the triangle inequality {#derive-the-triangle-inequality}

Expand the square, then apply Cauchy–Schwarz:
\begin{align*}
\|\vct{u}+\vct{v}\|^2
&=\|\vct{u}\|^2+2\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle+\|\vct{v}\|^2\\
&\le\|\vct{u}\|^2+2\|\vct{u}\|\|\vct{v}\|+\|\vct{v}\|^2\\
&=(\|\vct{u}\|+\|\vct{v}\|)^2
\end{align*}

Both sides are nonnegative, so take square roots

Cauchy–Schwarz also puts the real angle formula's cosine in $[-1,1]$

:::


# Orthogonality and Projection {#orthogonality-and-projection}

- [Projection onto one direction](#projection-onto-one-direction)
- [Projection onto an orthonormal basis](#projection-onto-an-orthonormal-basis)

## Perpendicular vectors split squared length {#perpendicular-vectors-split-squared-length}

$\vct{u}\perp\vct{v}$ means $\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle=0$
\begin{equation*}
\|\vct{u}+\vct{v}\|^2=\|\vct{u}\|^2+\|\vct{v}\|^2
\end{equation*}

Nonzero pairwise orthogonal vectors are linearly independent

An orthonormal list is pairwise orthogonal with each vector of norm one

::: {.notes}
For independence, take the inner product of a zero linear combination with each list vector. Its coefficient times the positive squared norm must vanish. The zero vector is perpendicular to every vector but cannot belong to an orthonormal list.
:::

---

### Expand the square and isolate each coefficient {#orthogonal-length-and-independence}

When $\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle=0$:
\begin{equation*}
\|\vct{u}+\vct{v}\|^2
=\|\vct{u}\|^2+2\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle+\|\vct{v}\|^2
=\|\vct{u}\|^2+\|\vct{v}\|^2
\end{equation*}

For nonzero pairwise orthogonal $\vct{u}_1,\ldots,\vct{u}_k$:
\begin{gather*}
\sum_{j=1}^k c_j\vct{u}_j=\vct{0}
\implies
0=\left\langle\vct{u}_i,\sum_{j=1}^kc_j\vct{u}_j\right\rangle
=c_i\|\vct{u}_i\|^2\\
\|\vct{u}_i\|^2>0\implies c_i=0\quad\text{for every }i
\end{gather*}


## Projection onto one direction {#projection-onto-one-direction}

Project the vector $\vct{v}$ onto the line through the origin in direction $\vct{u}\ne\vct{0}$
\begin{equation*}
L=\operatorname{span}\{\vct{u}\}=\{c\vct{u}:c\in\reals\}
\end{equation*}

The projection $\vct{p}$ lies on $L$; the residual $\vct{r}$ is perpendicular to $L$
\begin{gather*}
\vct{p}=\frac{\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle}{\langle\vct{u},\vct{u}\rangle}\vct{u},\qquad
\vct{r}=\vct{v}-\vct{p}\\
\vct{p}\in\operatorname{span}\{\vct{u}\},\qquad \vct{r}\perp\vct{u}
\end{gather*}

For every candidate $\vct{w}\in L$:
\begin{equation*}
\|\vct{v}-\vct{w}\|^2=\|\vct{r}\|^2+\|\vct{p}-\vct{w}\|^2
\end{equation*}

$\vct{p}$ is the unique vector in $L$ closest to $\vct{v}$

---

### Orthogonality determines the projection coefficient {#derive-the-line-projection}

Write $\vct{p}=c\vct{u}$ and require $\vct{r}=\vct{v}-c\vct{u}\perp\vct{u}$
\begin{align*}
0&=\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}-c\vct{u}\rangle
=\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle-c\langle\vct{u},\vct{u}\rangle\\
c&=\frac{\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle}{\langle\vct{u},\vct{u}\rangle}
\end{align*}

For any other $\vct{w}\in L$, the difference $\vct{p}-\vct{w}$ also lies in $L$
\begin{gather*}
\vct{v}-\vct{w}=\vct{r}+(\vct{p}-\vct{w}),\qquad
\vct{r}\perp(\vct{p}-\vct{w})\\
\|\vct{v}-\vct{w}\|^2=\|\vct{r}\|^2+\|\vct{p}-\vct{w}\|^2\ge\|\vct{r}\|^2
\end{gather*}

Equality holds only for $\vct{w}=\vct{p}$



---

### Example: project onto the line $x_2=x_1$ {#line-projection-worked-example}

Use the standard dot product, $\vct{u}=[1,1]^\top$, and $\vct{v}=[3,1]^\top$
\begin{gather*}
L=\{c[1,1]^\top:c\in\reals\}=\{[c,c]^\top:c\in\reals\}\\
c=\frac{\vct{u}^\top\vct{v}}{\vct{u}^\top\vct{u}}
=\frac{1\cdot3+1\cdot1}{1^2+1^2}=2\\
\vct{p}=2\vct{u}=[2,2]^\top,\qquad
\vct{r}=\vct{v}-\vct{p}=[1,-1]^\top\\
\vct{u}^\top\vct{r}=1-1=0,\qquad d(\vct{v},L)=\|\vct{r}\|=\sqrt2
\end{gather*}

The closest point to $(3,1)$ on $x_2=x_1$ is $(2,2)$

## Projection onto an orthonormal basis {#projection-onto-an-orthonormal-basis}

Let $V$ be a real inner-product space and $S\subseteq V$ a finite-dimensional subspace

Let $\{\vct{q}_1,\ldots,\vct{q}_k\}$ be an orthonormal basis of $S$

For any $\vct{v}\in V$, its projection onto $S$ is
\begin{gather*}
\vct{p}=\operatorname{proj}_S\vct{v}=\sum_{j=1}^k\langle\vct{q}_j,\vct{v}\rangle\vct{q}_j\\
\vct{v}=\vct{p}+\vct{r},\qquad \vct{p}\in S,\quad \vct{r}\in S^\perp
\end{gather*}

Here $S^\perp=\{\vct{r}\in V:\langle\vct{r},\vct{s}\rangle=0\text{ for every }\vct{s}\in S\}$

Orthonormal coordinates require inner products instead of solving a new system

---

### Extract the coefficients and verify the residual {#derive-the-subspace-projection}

For $\vct{v}\in V$, seek $\vct{p}\in S$: write $\vct{p}=\sum_jc_j\vct{q}_j$ and impose $\vct{v}-\vct{p}\perp S$
\begin{align*}
0&=\left\langle\vct{q}_i,\vct{v}-\sum_jc_j\vct{q}_j\right\rangle
=\langle\vct{q}_i,\vct{v}\rangle-c_i\\
c_i&=\langle\vct{q}_i,\vct{v}\rangle,\qquad
\langle\vct{q}_i,\vct{r}\rangle=0\quad\text{for every }i
\end{align*}

Every vector in $S$ is a combination of the $\vct{q}_i$, so $\vct{r}\perp S$
\begin{equation*}
\|\vct{v}-\vct{w}\|^2
=\|\vct{r}\|^2+\|\vct{p}-\vct{w}\|^2\quad(\vct{w}\in S)
\end{equation*}

The same closest-point argument works for the whole subspace


## An orthogonal projector has two signatures {#an-orthogonal-projector-has-two-signatures}

In standard Euclidean coordinates, let $\mat{Q}$ have orthonormal columns spanning $S$
\begin{gather*}
\mat{P}=\mat{Q}\mat{Q}^\top,\qquad
\mat{P}^\top=\mat{P},\quad\mat{P}^2=\mat{P}\\
\mat{P}\vct{v}\in S,\qquad (\mat{I}-\mat{P})\vct{v}\in S^\perp
\end{gather*}

Idempotence alone characterizes a projection; symmetry additionally makes it orthogonal

[Revisit concrete projections]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}})

::: {.notes}
The symmetry criterion assumes the standard dot product. In a W inner product, the corresponding criterion is P^T W = W P together with idempotence. Finite-dimensional subspaces admit the orthogonal decomposition used here.
:::

---

### Verify the projector identities {#verify-the-projector-identities}

Since $\mat{Q}^\top\mat{Q}=\mat{I}_k$:
\begin{align*}
\mat{P}^\top&=(\mat{Q}\mat{Q}^\top)^\top=\mat{Q}\mat{Q}^\top=\mat{P}\\
\mat{P}^2&=\mat{Q}(\mat{Q}^\top\mat{Q})\mat{Q}^\top=\mat{Q}\mat{Q}^\top=\mat{P}\\
\mat{Q}^\top(\mat{I}-\mat{P})\vct{v}
&=\mat{Q}^\top\vct{v}-(\mat{Q}^\top\mat{Q})\mat{Q}^\top\vct{v}=\vct{0}
\end{align*}

Conversely, if $\mat{P}^2=\mat{P}=\mat{P}^\top$, then
\begin{equation*}
(\mat{P}\vct{x})^\top(\mat{I}-\mat{P})\vct{y}
=\vct{x}^\top(\mat{P}-\mat{P}^2)\vct{y}=0
\end{equation*}

Its range and residual directions are perpendicular

- [A worked Gram–Schmidt calculation](#a-worked-gram-schmidt-calculation)
- [The coefficients form a triangular matrix](#the-coefficients-form-a-triangular-matrix)
- [Read QR from the worked example](#read-qr-from-the-worked-example)

## Build perpendicular directions without changing the span {#build-perpendicular-directions-without-changing-the-span}

Start with independent $\vct{A}_1,\ldots,\vct{A}_n$
\begin{align*}
\vct{w}_1&=\vct{A}_1,\qquad\vct{q}_1=\vct{w}_1/\|\vct{w}_1\|\\
\vct{w}_j&=\vct{A}_j-\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\langle\vct{q}_i,\vct{A}_j\rangle\vct{q}_i\\
\vct{q}_j&=\vct{w}_j/\|\vct{w}_j\|
\end{align*}

At each step, remove directions already represented, then normalize

$\operatorname{span}\{\vct{q}_1,\ldots,\vct{q}_j\}=\operatorname{span}\{\vct{A}_1,\ldots,\vct{A}_j\}$

---

### Why the Gram–Schmidt step works {#why-the-gram-schmidt-step-works}

For $\ell<j$, orthonormality cancels all but one term:
\begin{equation*}
\langle\vct{q}_\ell,\vct{w}_j\rangle
=\langle\vct{q}_\ell,\vct{A}_j\rangle
-\sum_{i<j}\langle\vct{q}_i,\vct{A}_j\rangle
\langle\vct{q}_\ell,\vct{q}_i\rangle=0
\end{equation*}

If $\vct{w}_j=\vct{0}$, then $\vct{A}_j$ lies in the preceding span

Independence rules this out, so normalization is possible
\begin{equation*}
\vct{A}_j=\sum_{i<j}\langle\vct{q}_i,\vct{A}_j\rangle\vct{q}_i
+\|\vct{w}_j\|\vct{q}_j
\end{equation*}

Each old vector uses only the new directions through its own step


## A worked Gram–Schmidt calculation {#a-worked-gram-schmidt-calculation}

In $\reals^3$, normalize the first column
\begin{equation*}
\vct{A}_1=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\vct{A}_2=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\vct{q}_1=\frac{\vct{A}_1}{\|\vct{A}_1\|}
=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{bmatrix}
\end{equation*}

Remove its component from the second column
\begin{align*}
\langle\vct{q}_1,\vct{A}_2\rangle
&=\frac{1\cdot1+1\cdot0+0\cdot1}{\sqrt2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\\
\vct{w}_2&=\vct{A}_2-\langle\vct{q}_1,\vct{A}_2\rangle\vct{q}_1\\
&=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}
-\frac12\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}1-1/2\\0-1/2\\1-0\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}1/2\\-1/2\\1\end{bmatrix}
\end{align*}

---

### Normalize the remainder and check orthonormality {#gram-schmidt-example-arithmetic}

Continue by normalizing the remainder $\vct{w}_2$ from the preceding slide
\begin{align*}
\|\vct{w}_2\|^2&=\frac14+\frac14+1=\frac32\\
\vct{q}_2&=\frac{\vct{w}_2}{\|\vct{w}_2\|}
=\sqrt{\frac23}\begin{bmatrix}1/2\\-1/2\\1\end{bmatrix}
=\frac1{\sqrt6}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{bmatrix}\\
\vct{q}_1^\top\vct{q}_2&=\frac{1-1+0}{\sqrt{12}}=0\\
\|\vct{q}_1\|^2&=\frac{1+1+0}{2}=1,\qquad
\|\vct{q}_2\|^2=\frac{1+1+4}{6}=1
\end{align*}

The two directions are perpendicular and each has length one


## The coefficients form a triangular matrix {#the-coefficients-form-a-triangular-matrix}

For a real $m\times n$ matrix with independent columns, $m\ge n$:
\begin{gather*}
\mat{A}=\mat{Q}\mat{R},\qquad \mat{Q}^\top\mat{Q}=\mat{I}_n\\
\mat{Q}=[\vct{q}_1\ \cdots\ \vct{q}_n],\qquad
(\mat{R})_{ij}=\begin{cases}\vct{q}_i^\top\vct{A}_j,&i\le j\\0,&i>j\end{cases}
\end{gather*}

$\mat{Q}$: $m\times n$ orthonormal directions

$\mat{R}$: $n\times n$ upper triangular coordinates, positive diagonal with this construction

Here $\mat{R}$ is the QR factor, different from $\mat{R}$ in $\mat{A}=\mat{C}\mat{R}$

::: {.notes}
This is reduced QR. Here R denotes the triangular QR factor, not the row-space factor in A=C R. Reused matrix letters are defined by the current factorization. When Q is rectangular, Q^T Q=I but Q Q^T is a projector rather than the identity.
:::


## Read QR from the worked example {#read-qr-from-the-worked-example}

\begin{gather*}
\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{Q}=\begin{bmatrix}
1/\sqrt2&1/\sqrt6\\1/\sqrt2&-1/\sqrt6\\0&2/\sqrt6
\end{bmatrix}\\
\mat{R}=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt2&1/\sqrt2\\0&\sqrt{3/2}\end{bmatrix}
\end{gather*}

Column 1 uses only $\vct{q}_1$; column 2 uses $\vct{q}_1$ and $\vct{q}_2$

Verify $\mat{Q}\mat{R}=\mat{A}$

---

### Recover each original column {#verify-the-worked-qr}

The Gram–Schmidt coefficients give
\begin{align*}
\vct{A}_1&=\sqrt2\vct{q}_1=[1,1,0]^\top\\
\vct{A}_2&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\vct{q}_1+\sqrt{\frac32}\vct{q}_2\\
&=\frac12[1,1,0]^\top+\frac12[1,-1,2]^\top
=[1,0,1]^\top
\end{align*}

These are exactly the columns of $\mat{Q}\mat{R}$

Multiplying $\mat{A}=\mat{Q}\mat{R}$ by $\mat{Q}^\top$ gives $\mat{R}=\mat{Q}^\top\mat{A}$


## Exact construction and numerical computation differ {#exact-construction-and-numerical-computation-differ}

- Dependent input: a zero remainder cannot be normalized
- Nearly dependent input: subtraction can lose orthogonality in floating point
- Modified Gram–Schmidt updates the remainder after each projection
- Householder QR uses orthogonal reflections for practical computation

[Recall Householder reflections]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}})

::: {.key-point}
Gram–Schmidt explains QR; numerical algorithms must also control round-off error
:::

::: {.notes}
Dependence detection in floating point requires a scale-aware tolerance; no universal fixed threshold is prescribed. Householder QR is backward stable; classical Gram–Schmidt may lose orthogonality substantially for ill-conditioned inputs. Reorthogonalization is another option.
:::


## Practice extracting QR coordinates {#practice-extracting-qr-coordinates}


::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Apply Gram–Schmidt to $[1,0,1]^\top$ and $[1,1,0]^\top$<br>Write the reduced QR factorization<br>Why is $\mat{Q}\mat{Q}^\top$ not $\mat{I}_3$?</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
q_1=[1,0,1]^T/sqrt(2), q_2=[1,2,-1]^T/sqrt(6), R=[[sqrt(2),1/sqrt(2)],[0,sqrt(3/2)]]. Q Q^T has rank two and projects onto the plane spanned by the two columns.
:::

- [Fit a line to three observations](#fit-a-line-to-three-observations)
- [Inspect the fit and residual](#inspect-the-fit-and-residual)
- [A line fit leaves vertical residuals](#regression-residual-figure)
- [General features keep the model linear in coefficients](#general-features-keep-the-model-linear-in-coefficients)

## Inconsistent systems still have a best fit {#inconsistent-systems-still-have-a-best-fit}

Minimize $\|\vct{b}-\mat{A}\vct{x}\|^2$ over coefficient vectors $\vct{x}$

Let $\vct{p}=\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{col}(\mat{A})}\vct{b}$ and $\vct{r}=\vct{b}-\vct{p}$

Write $\vct{b}-\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{r}+(\vct{p}-\mat{A}\vct{x})$

The last term is in $\operatorname{col}(\mat{A})$ and $\vct{r}$ is perpendicular to that space
\begin{equation*}
\|\vct{b}-\mat{A}\vct{x}\|^2
=\|\vct{r}\|^2+\|\vct{p}-\mat{A}\vct{x}\|^2
\end{equation*}

The minimum occurs exactly when $\mat{A}\widehat{\vct{x}}=\vct{p}$

Each column of $\mat{A}$ is perpendicular to $\vct{r}$, giving the [normal equations]{.alert}
\begin{equation*}
\mat{A}^\top\vct{r}=\vct{0}
\implies
\mat{A}^\top(\vct{b}-\mat{A}\widehat{\vct{x}})=\vct{0}
\implies
\mat{A}^\top\mat{A}\widehat{\vct{x}}=\mat{A}^\top\vct{b}
\end{equation*}

Unique fitted vector, with unique coefficients exactly when the columns are independent


## QR turns least squares into a triangular solve {#qr-turns-least-squares-into-a-triangular-solve}

For $\mat{A}$ with independent columns, reduced QR has $m\ge n$ and
\begin{equation*}
\underset{m\times n}{\mat{A}}=\underset{m\times n}{\mat{Q}}\,\underset{n\times n}{\mat{R}},
\qquad \mat{Q}^\top\mat{Q}=\mat{I}_n
\end{equation*}

When $m>n$, both $\mat{A}$ and $\mat{Q}$ are rectangular. Then $\mat{Q}^\top$ is a left inverse, and $\mat{Q}^{-1}$ does not exist

$\mat{Q}\mat{Q}^\top$ projects onto $\operatorname{col}(\mat{A})$. Only in the square case is $\mat{Q}^\top=\mat{Q}^{-1}$

[The projection coordinates are $\vct{c}=\mat{Q}^\top\vct{b}$, so $\vct{p}=\mat{Q}\vct{c}$]{#the-projection-formula-reconnects-earlier-geometry}
\begin{align*}
\mat{A}\widehat{\vct{x}}&=\vct{p}\\
\mat{Q}\mat{R}\widehat{\vct{x}}&=\mat{Q}\vct{c}\\
(\mat{Q}^\top\mat{Q})\mat{R}\widehat{\vct{x}}&=(\mat{Q}^\top\mat{Q})\vct{c}\\
\mat{R}\widehat{\vct{x}}&=\vct{c}=\mat{Q}^\top\vct{b}
\end{align*}

$\mat{R}$ is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal, so solve from the last row upward

::: {.notes}
This calculation solves for the coefficients that produce the best fitted vector established on the previous slide. The projection matrix is QQ^T. Solving the normal equations symbolically and multiplying the result by A gives the equivalent projector A(A^T A)^{-1}A^T. QR uses only the projection coordinates and a triangular solve.
:::


## Fit a line to three observations {#fit-a-line-to-three-observations}

Fit $b\approx x_1+x_2t$ to $(t,b)=(-1,1),(0,0),(1,2)$
\begin{equation*}
\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\1&0\\1&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\vct{b}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{bmatrix}
\end{equation*}

The column dot product is $-1+0+1=0$

Divide the columns by their lengths $\sqrt3$ and $\sqrt2$ to form $\mat{Q}$
\begin{equation*}
\mat{R}=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt3&0\\0&\sqrt2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{Q}^\top\vct{b}
=\begin{bmatrix}(1+0+2)/\sqrt3\\(-1+0+2)/\sqrt2\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt3\\1/\sqrt2\end{bmatrix}
\end{equation*}

Solve the bottom row first: $\sqrt2\,\widehat{x}_2=1/\sqrt2$, then $\sqrt3\,\widehat{x}_1=\sqrt3$

The fitted line is $\widehat b(t)=1+t/2$


## Inspect the fit and residual {#inspect-the-fit-and-residual}

Evaluate the fitted line at $t=-1,0,1$ and subtract from the observations
\begin{align*}
\widehat{\vct{b}}
&=\begin{bmatrix}1-1/2\\1\\1+1/2\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}1/2\\1\\3/2\end{bmatrix}\\
\vct{r}
&=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{bmatrix}-\widehat{\vct{b}}
=\begin{bmatrix}1/2\\-1\\1/2\end{bmatrix}\\
\mat{A}^\top\vct{r}
&=\begin{bmatrix}1/2-1+1/2\\-1/2+0+1/2\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\|\vct{r}\|^2=1/4+1+1/4=3/2
\end{align*}

The residual is perpendicular to both feature columns: the ones and the sampled $t$ values


## A line fit leaves vertical residuals {#regression-residual-figure}

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
![](assets/special-topics/regression-residuals.svg){fig-alt="Three observations at t equals minus one, zero, and one, with response values one, zero, and two. The fitted line is one plus t over two. Dashed vertical segments show the residuals." width="76%" .nostretch}
:::

Least squares minimizes the sum of squared vertical errors


## General features keep the model linear in coefficients {#general-features-keep-the-model-linear-in-coefficients}

Choose features $\phi_1(t),\ldots,\phi_n(t)$
\begin{gather*}
\widehat b(t)=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\phi_j(t),\qquad a_{ij}=\phi_j(t_i)
\end{gather*}

- Polynomial regression: $1,t,t^2,\ldots$
- Periodic features: sines and cosines
- Several predictors: one column for each chosen feature

::: {.key-point}
Linear regression means linear in the unknown coefficients
:::

::: {.notes}
A feature may be nonlinear in t. Least squares alone does not establish causation or predictive performance. More features can improve training fit while worsening generalization; use held-out data when the goal is prediction.
:::


## Weighted least squares rescales the rows {#weights-and-rank-deficiency-change-the-calculation}

Give observation $i$ weight $w_i>0$ and set $\mat{W}=\operatorname{diag}(w_1,\ldots,w_m)$

Multiply row $i$ of $\mat{A}$ and entry $i$ of $\vct{b}$ by $\sqrt{w_i}$
\begin{align*}
\widetilde{\mat{A}}&=\mat{W}^{1/2}\mat{A},\qquad
\widetilde{\vct{b}}=\mat{W}^{1/2}\vct{b}\\
\sum_i w_i\bigl((\mat{A}\vct{x})_i-b_i\bigr)^2
&=\|\widetilde{\mat{A}}\vct{x}-\widetilde{\vct{b}}\|^2
\end{align*}

Use ordinary least squares on the rescaled data. The residual condition becomes
\begin{equation*}
\widetilde{\mat{A}}^\top(\widetilde{\vct{b}}-\widetilde{\mat{A}}\widehat{\vct{x}})
=\mat{A}^\top\mat{W}(\vct{b}-\mat{A}\widehat{\vct{x}})=\vct{0}
\end{equation*}

Dependent or nearly dependent features motivate [SVD and regularization](#regression-through-qr-and-svd)


## Practice checking a regression fit {#practice-checking-a-regression-fit}


::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Fit $b\approx x_1+x_2t$ to $(-1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$<br>Find coefficients, fitted values, and residuals<br>Check both normal equations</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Coefficients [2/3,1/2]^T. Fitted values [1/6,2/3,7/6]^T; residuals [-1/6,1/3,-1/6]^T. Sum of residuals and dot product with [-1,0,1]^T are zero. Squared residual norm is 1/6.
:::


# Singular Value Decomposition {#singular-value-decomposition}

Orthogonal input and output coordinates extend the eigenvector idea to rectangular matrices

- [What can a rectangular matrix do?](#what-can-a-rectangular-matrix-do)
- [The SVD separates directions from scale](#the-svd-separates-directions-from-scale)
- [Each singular direction has its own stretch](#each-singular-direction-has-its-own-stretch)
- [A worked SVD without square roots of large matrices](#a-worked-svd-without-square-roots-of-large-matrices)
- [See the singular stretches](#svd-geometry)
- [Why an SVD exists](#why-an-svd-exists)
- [The four spaces reappear in orthonormal coordinates](#the-four-spaces-reappear-in-orthonormal-coordinates)
- [A matrix is a sum of rank-one maps](#a-matrix-is-a-sum-of-rank-one-maps)
- [The best low-rank approximation has a measurable error](#the-best-low-rank-approximation-has-a-measurable-error)
- [Practice reading singular values](#practice-reading-singular-values)

## What can a rectangular matrix do? {#what-can-a-rectangular-matrix-do}

$\mat{A}:\reals^n\to\reals^m$ may stretch, turn, and collapse directions

Eigenvectors require a square matrix; singular vectors work for every shape

::: {.key-point}
Choose orthonormal input and output directions adapted to the map
:::


## The SVD separates directions from scale {#the-svd-separates-directions-from-scale}

For a real $m\times n$ matrix of rank $r>0$:
\begin{gather*}
\mat{A}=\mat{U}_r\mat{\Sigma}_r\mat{V}_r^\top,\qquad
\mat{\Sigma}_r=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r)\\
\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0,\qquad
\mat{U}_r^\top\mat{U}_r=\mat{V}_r^\top\mat{V}_r=\mat{I}_r
\end{gather*}

| Factor | Shape | Role |
|---|---|---|
| $\mat{V}_r^\top$ | $r\times n$ | input coordinates |
| $\mat{\Sigma}_r$ | $r\times r$ | stretch each coordinate |
| $\mat{U}_r$ | $m\times r$ | assemble the output |

::: {.notes}
This is the compact SVD. The zero matrix has no positive singular values and an empty compact factorization; its pseudoinverse is zero. Orthogonal completions give the full SVD with U m-by-m, V n-by-n, and rectangular Sigma.
:::


## Each singular direction has its own stretch {#each-singular-direction-has-its-own-stretch}

Write $\vct{U}_j$ and $\vct{V}_j$ for columns of the compact factors
\begin{gather*}
\mat{A}\vct{V}_j=\sigma_j\vct{U}_j,\qquad
\mat{A}^\top\vct{U}_j=\sigma_j\vct{V}_j\\
\mat{A}\vct{x}=\sum_{j=1}^r\sigma_j\vct{U}_j
\bigl(\vct{V}_j^\top\vct{x}\bigr)
\end{gather*}

Input perpendicular to every $\vct{V}_j$ is sent to zero

::: {.key-point}
Singular values measure stretches, not signed eigenvalues
:::


## A worked SVD without square roots of large matrices {#a-worked-svd-without-square-roots-of-large-matrices}

\begin{gather*}
\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix},\quad
\mat{U}_r=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\quad
\mat{\Sigma}_r=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix},\quad
\mat{V}_r=\mat{I}_2\\
\mat{A}\begin{bmatrix}\cos t\\\sin t\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}3\cos t\\0\\2\sin t\end{bmatrix}
\end{gather*}

The unit circle becomes an ellipse in the $x_1x_3$ plane

::: {.key-point}
The ellipse axes are the left singular vectors; their lengths are the singular values
:::


## See the singular stretches {#svd-geometry}

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
![](assets/special-topics/svd-circle-ellipse.svg){fig-alt="The unit input circle maps to an ellipse with semiaxes three and two in the output x1 x3 plane" width="90%" .nostretch}
:::

## Why an SVD exists {#why-an-svd-exists}

$\mat{A}^\top\mat{A}$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite
\begin{gather*}
\vct{x}^\top\mat{A}^\top\mat{A}\vct{x}
=\|\mat{A}\vct{x}\|^2\ge0\\
\mat{A}^\top\mat{A}\vct{V}_j=\sigma_j^2\vct{V}_j,\qquad
\vct{U}_j=\frac{\mat{A}\vct{V}_j}{\sigma_j}\quad(\sigma_j>0)
\end{gather*}

Orthonormal eigenvectors on the input side produce orthonormal output vectors

::: {.notes}
For positive singular values, U_i^T U_j = V_i^T A^T A V_j/(sigma_i sigma_j) = delta_ij. Use the real symmetric spectral theorem from Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors; the optional quadratic-forms section is not a prerequisite. This is an existence argument, not a recommended numerical algorithm: forming A^T A squares the full-column-rank condition number.
:::

---

### Verify orthonormality and reconstruct the map {#complete-the-svd-existence-argument}

Choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $\mat{A}^\top\mat{A}$

For positive eigenvalues $\sigma_j^2$, set $\vct{U}_j=\mat{A}\vct{V}_j/\sigma_j$
\begin{equation*}
\vct{U}_i^\top\vct{U}_j
=\frac{\vct{V}_i^\top\mat{A}^\top\mat{A}\vct{V}_j}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}
=\frac{\sigma_j^2\vct{V}_i^\top\vct{V}_j}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}
=\begin{cases}1,&i=j\\0,&i\ne j\end{cases}
\end{equation*}

A zero eigenvalue gives $\|\mat{A}\vct{V}_j\|^2=0$, hence $\mat{A}\vct{V}_j=\vct{0}$
\begin{equation*}
\mat{A}\vct{x}
=\mat{A}\sum_{j=1}^n\vct{V}_j(\vct{V}_j^\top\vct{x})
=\sum_{j=1}^r\sigma_j\vct{U}_j(\vct{V}_j^\top\vct{x})
\end{equation*}


## The four spaces reappear in orthonormal coordinates {#the-four-spaces-reappear-in-orthonormal-coordinates}

| Space | SVD description |
|---|---|
| $\operatorname{col}(\mat{A})$ | span of $\vct{U}_1,\ldots,\vct{U}_r$ |
| $\operatorname{row}(\mat{A})$ | span of $\vct{V}_1,\ldots,\vct{V}_r$ |
| $\operatorname{null}(\mat{A})$ | perpendicular to all $\vct{V}_j$ |
| $\operatorname{null}(\mat{A}^\top)$ | perpendicular to all $\vct{U}_j$ |

Complete the columns of $\mat{U}_r$ and $\mat{V}_r$ to orthonormal bases to obtain bases of the two null spaces

[Recall matrix spaces]({{< meta decks.d08.file >}}#orthogonal-pairs)


## A matrix is a sum of rank-one maps {#a-matrix-is-a-sum-of-rank-one-maps}

\begin{equation*}
\mat{A}=\sum_{j=1}^r\sigma_j\vct{U}_j\vct{V}_j^\top
\end{equation*}

Each term reads one input coordinate and sends it along one output direction

Keep only the first $k$ terms:
\begin{equation*}
\mat{A}_k=\sum_{j=1}^k\sigma_j\vct{U}_j\vct{V}_j^\top,\qquad 0\le k<r
\end{equation*}

A controlled approximation using fewer directions


## The best low-rank approximation has a measurable error {#the-best-low-rank-approximation-has-a-measurable-error}

Define $\|\mat{B}\|_F^2=\sum_{i,j}|b_{ij}|^2$ and
$\|\mat{B}\|_2=\max_{\|\vct{x}\|=1}\|\mat{B}\vct{x}\|$
\begin{gather*}
\|\mat{A}-\mat{A}_k\|_2=\sigma_{k+1}\\
\|\mat{A}-\mat{A}_k\|_F^2=\sum_{j=k+1}^r\sigma_j^2
\end{gather*}

$\mat{A}_k$ minimizes either error over matrices of rank at most $k$

::: {.key-point}
Choose the rank by the accuracy needed, not only by the appearance of the image
:::

::: {.notes}
The continuation derives both tail-error formulas and spectral optimality; Frobenius optimality is stated without proof (Eckart–Young–Mirsky). Approximation need not be unique when singular values tie. For an m-by-n grayscale image, storing compact factors uses k(m+n+1) scalar entries instead of mn, before file-format overhead or quantization.
:::

---

### Compute the discarded-tail errors {#derive-the-svd-tail-errors}

Let $\mat{E}=\mat{A}-\mat{A}_k=\sum_{j>k}\sigma_j\vct{U}_j\vct{V}_j^\top$
\begin{align*}
\|\mat{E}\vct{x}\|^2
&=\sum_{j>k}\sigma_j^2|\vct{V}_j^\top\vct{x}|^2
\le\sigma_{k+1}^2\|\vct{x}\|^2\\
\|\mat{E}\vct{V}_{k+1}\|&=\sigma_{k+1}
\end{align*}

Thus $\|\mat{E}\|_2=\sigma_{k+1}$

The rank-one terms are orthonormal in the Frobenius inner product:
\begin{gather*}
\sum_{a,b}(U_{ai}V_{bi})(U_{aj}V_{bj})
=(\vct{U}_i^\top\vct{U}_j)(\vct{V}_i^\top\vct{V}_j)\\
\|\mat{E}\|_F^2=\sum_{j>k}\sigma_j^2
\end{gather*}

---

### Why no rank-$k$ matrix improves the spectral error {#why-the-svd-spectral-approximation-is-best}

Let $\operatorname{rank}(\mat{B})\le k$ and $T=\operatorname{span}\{\vct{V}_1,\ldots,\vct{V}_{k+1}\}$

A map of rank at most $k$ cannot be one-to-one on this $(k+1)$-dimensional space

Choose $\vct{x}\in T$ with $\|\vct{x}\|=1$ and $\mat{B}\vct{x}=\vct{0}$
\begin{align*}
\|\mat{A}-\mat{B}\|_2^2
&\ge\|(\mat{A}-\mat{B})\vct{x}\|^2=\|\mat{A}\vct{x}\|^2\\
&=\sum_{j=1}^{k+1}\sigma_j^2|\vct{V}_j^\top\vct{x}|^2
\ge\sigma_{k+1}^2
\end{align*}

The truncated SVD attains this lower bound

Frobenius optimality is the companion Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem; its proof is omitted


## Practice reading singular values {#practice-reading-singular-values}


::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>A matrix has singular values $8,3,1$<br>Find the rank-one spectral error and rank-two Frobenius error<br>How many rank-one terms reproduce the matrix exactly?</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Answers: 3; 1; three terms. Distinguish the two error norms.
:::

- [The pseudoinverse reverses the nonzero stretches](#the-pseudoinverse-reverses-the-nonzero-stretches)
- [Rank deficiency changes coefficients, not the fitted vector](#rank-deficiency-changes-coefficients-not-the-fitted-vector)
- [A regression example with a redundant feature](#a-regression-example-with-a-redundant-feature)
- [Small singular values amplify data perturbations](#small-singular-values-amplify-data-perturbations)
- [Truncation and ridge control small stretches](#truncation-and-ridge-control-small-stretches)
- [Which factorization serves the regression question?](#which-factorization-serves-the-regression-question)
- [Practice separating fit from coefficients](#practice-separating-fit-from-coefficients)

## Regression asks for the closest attainable data {#regression-asks-for-the-closest-attainable-data}

Fit observations $b_i$ using features $a_{ij}$ and coefficients $x_j$
\begin{gather*}
\widehat{\vct{b}}=\mat{A}\widehat{\vct{x}},\qquad
\widehat{\vct{x}}\in\arg\min_{\vct{x}}\|\mat{A}\vct{x}-\vct{b}\|^2\\
\mat{A}^\top(\vct{b}-\widehat{\vct{b}})=\vct{0}
\end{gather*}

$\widehat{\vct{b}}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{col}(\mat{A})$

A column of ones supplies an intercept

[Recall least squares](#least-squares-and-regression)


## QR solves full-column-rank least squares {#qr-solves-full-column-rank-least-squares}

For $m\ge n$ and independent columns:
\begin{gather*}
\mat{A}=\mat{Q}\mat{R},\quad
\mat{Q}^\top\mat{Q}=\mat{I}_n,\quad
\mat{R}\text{ upper triangular and invertible}\\
\|\mat{A}\vct{x}-\vct{b}\|^2
=\|\mat{R}\vct{x}-\mat{Q}^\top\vct{b}\|^2
+\|(\mat{I}_m-\mat{Q}\mat{Q}^\top)\vct{b}\|^2\\
\mat{R}\widehat{\vct{x}}=\mat{Q}^\top\vct{b}
\end{gather*}

Compute orthogonal coordinates, then use back substitution

::: {.notes}
Reduced QR: Q is m-by-n, R is n-by-n. This R is the triangular QR factor, different from R in A=C R; reused matrix letters are defined by the current factorization. Gram–Schmidt explains the factorization; Householder QR is the standard practical method. This is an optional refresher of the earlier QR section; skip these two recap slides when proceeding directly to the pseudoinverse.
:::


## The pseudoinverse reverses the nonzero stretches {#the-pseudoinverse-reverses-the-nonzero-stretches}

\begin{gather*}
\mat{A}^{\dagger}=\mat{V}_r\mat{\Sigma}_r^{-1}\mat{U}_r^\top\\
\widehat{\vct{x}}=\mat{A}^{\dagger}\vct{b}
=\sum_{j=1}^r\frac{\vct{U}_j^\top\vct{b}}{\sigma_j}\vct{V}_j\\
\widehat{\vct{b}}=\mat{A}\widehat{\vct{x}}
=\mat{U}_r\mat{U}_r^\top\vct{b}
\end{gather*}

Works for rectangular and rank-deficient matrices

::: {.key-point}
The pseudoinverse selects the least-squares solution with smallest Euclidean norm
:::

---

### Minimize one singular coordinate at a time {#derive-the-pseudoinverse-fit}

Split $\vct{b}=\sum_{j=1}^r\beta_j\vct{U}_j+\vct{b}_\perp$, where $\beta_j=\vct{U}_j^\top\vct{b}$

Write $\vct{x}=\sum_{j=1}^r\alpha_j\vct{V}_j+\vct{z}$ with $\vct{z}\in\operatorname{null}(\mat{A})$
\begin{equation*}
\|\mat{A}\vct{x}-\vct{b}\|^2
=\sum_{j=1}^r(\sigma_j\alpha_j-\beta_j)^2+\|\vct{b}_\perp\|^2
\end{equation*}

Each square vanishes at $\alpha_j=\beta_j/\sigma_j$; $\vct{z}$ cannot change the fit
\begin{gather*}
\widehat{\vct{x}}=\sum_{j=1}^r\frac{\beta_j}{\sigma_j}\vct{V}_j
=\mat{V}_r\mat{\Sigma}_r^{-1}\mat{U}_r^\top\vct{b}\\
\mat{A}\widehat{\vct{x}}=\sum_{j=1}^r\beta_j\vct{U}_j=\mat{U}_r\mat{U}_r^\top\vct{b}
\end{gather*}


## Rank deficiency changes coefficients, not the fitted vector {#rank-deficiency-changes-coefficients-not-the-fitted-vector}

Every least-squares minimizer has the form
\begin{equation*}
\vct{x}=\mat{A}^{\dagger}\vct{b}+\vct{z},\qquad
\vct{z}\in\operatorname{null}(\mat{A})
\end{equation*}

- All give the same fitted vector $\widehat{\vct{b}}$
- The pseudoinverse solution lies in $\operatorname{row}(\mat{A})$
- Adding a perpendicular null-space component increases the coefficient norm

::: {.notes}
Use the orthogonal splitting R^n = row(A) plus null(A). The minimizer is unique exactly when A has full column rank. This also covers underdetermined consistent systems.
:::

---

### Separate coefficient freedom from the minimum norm {#derive-the-minimum-norm-property}

For $\vct{x}_*=\mat{A}^{\dagger}\vct{b}\in\operatorname{row}(\mat{A})$ and
$\vct{z}\in\operatorname{null}(\mat{A})$:
\begin{gather*}
\mat{A}(\vct{x}_*+\vct{z})=\mat{A}\vct{x}_*,\qquad \vct{x}_*\perp\vct{z}\\
\|\vct{x}_*+\vct{z}\|^2=\|\vct{x}_*\|^2+\|\vct{z}\|^2\ge\|\vct{x}_*\|^2
\end{gather*}

Equality holds only when $\vct{z}=\vct{0}$

Conversely, all minimizers share the unique projected fitted vector
\begin{equation*}
\mat{A}\vct{x}=\mat{A}\vct{x}_*\implies\vct{x}-\vct{x}_*\in\operatorname{null}(\mat{A})
\end{equation*}


## A regression example with a redundant feature {#a-regression-example-with-a-redundant-feature}

\begin{gather*}
\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix},\quad
\vct{b}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\4\end{bmatrix},\quad
\vct{U}_1=\vct{V}_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix},\quad\sigma_1=2\\
\widehat{\vct{x}}=\begin{bmatrix}3/2\\3/2\end{bmatrix},\quad
\widehat{\vct{b}}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\3\end{bmatrix},\quad
\vct{b}-\widehat{\vct{b}}=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}
\end{gather*}

Both features are identical: only $x_1+x_2=3$ is identifiable

The smallest-norm solution divides the total equally

---

### Compute the identifiable sum and its split {#redundant-feature-example-arithmetic}

The single nonzero singular coordinate is
\begin{gather*}
\beta_1=\vct{U}_1^\top\vct{b}=\frac{2+4}{\sqrt2}=3\sqrt2\\
\widehat{\vct{x}}=\frac{\beta_1}{\sigma_1}\vct{V}_1
=\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}3/2\\3/2\end{bmatrix}
\end{gather*}

Equivalently, put $s=x_1+x_2$ and complete the square:
\begin{equation*}
\|\mat{A}\vct{x}-\vct{b}\|^2=(s-2)^2+(s-4)^2=2(s-3)^2+2
\end{equation*}

Only the sum $s=3$ is determined by the data


## Small singular values amplify data perturbations {#small-singular-values-amplify-data-perturbations}

A perturbation $\delta\vct{b}$ changes the pseudoinverse coefficients by
\begin{equation*}
\delta\widehat{\vct{x}}
=\sum_{j=1}^r\frac{\vct{U}_j^\top\delta\vct{b}}{\sigma_j}\vct{V}_j
\end{equation*}

Small positive $\sigma_j$: large coefficient changes in direction $\vct{V}_j$

For full column rank, the 2-norm condition number is $\kappa(\mat{A})=\sigma_1/\sigma_n$

::: {.key-point}
An accurate fit can coexist with poorly determined coefficients
:::

::: {.notes}
For a general square matrix, use singular values, not eigenvalues, in the 2-norm condition number. For a real symmetric positive-definite matrix, singular values equal its positive eigenvalues, so the largest/smallest eigenvalue ratio is valid. Keep rank and conditioning distinct. Exact zero singular values create nonidentifiability; small positive ones create sensitivity. Feature scaling affects these values and the meaning of a coefficient-norm penalty.
:::


## Truncation and ridge control small stretches {#truncation-and-ridge-control-small-stretches}

Truncated SVD retains only singular values above a chosen threshold $\tau$:
\begin{equation*}
\widehat{\vct{x}}_\tau
=\sum_{\sigma_j>\tau}\frac{\vct{U}_j^\top\vct{b}}{\sigma_j}\vct{V}_j
\end{equation*}

Ridge minimizes $\|\mat{A}\vct{x}-\vct{b}\|^2+\lambda\|\vct{x}\|^2$, $\lambda>0$:
\begin{equation*}
\widehat{\vct{x}}_\lambda
=\sum_{j=1}^r\frac{\sigma_j}{\sigma_j^2+\lambda}
(\vct{U}_j^\top\vct{b})\vct{V}_j
\end{equation*}

Truncation discards directions; ridge shrinks their contributions

::: {.notes}
This ridge formula penalizes every coefficient, including an intercept if present. In typical regression, center features and response or explicitly exempt the intercept; then the formula must be applied to the corresponding centered or weighted-penalty problem. Parameter choice requires a noise model or validation data; this deck introduces the algebra only.
:::

---

### Derive the ridge shrinkage factor {#derive-the-ridge-shrinkage-factor}

Use the same singular coordinates $\alpha_j,\beta_j$ and null-space part $\vct{z}$
\begin{equation*}
\|\mat{A}\vct{x}-\vct{b}\|^2+\lambda\|\vct{x}\|^2
=\sum_{j=1}^r\bigl[(\sigma_j\alpha_j-\beta_j)^2+\lambda\alpha_j^2\bigr]
+\|\vct{b}_\perp\|^2+\lambda\|\vct{z}\|^2
\end{equation*}

For each coordinate, complete the square:
\begin{align*}
(\sigma\alpha-\beta)^2+\lambda\alpha^2
&=(\sigma^2+\lambda)\left(\alpha-\frac{\sigma\beta}{\sigma^2+\lambda}\right)^2
+\frac{\lambda\beta^2}{\sigma^2+\lambda}\\
\alpha_j&=\frac{\sigma_j\beta_j}{\sigma_j^2+\lambda},\qquad\vct{z}=\vct{0}
\end{align*}

Each pseudoinverse coordinate is multiplied by $\sigma_j^2/(\sigma_j^2+\lambda)$


## Which factorization serves the regression question? {#which-factorization-serves-the-regression-question}

| Question | Useful tool |
|---|---|
| Full-column-rank least-squares coefficients | QR and a triangular solve |
| Rank deficiency and minimum-norm coefficients | SVD and pseudoinverse |
| Sensitivity and numerical rank | Singular values and feature scaling |
| Noise-sensitive directions | Truncation or ridge |

Forming $\mat{A}^\top\mat{A}$ squares $\kappa(\mat{A})$ when $\mat{A}$ has full column rank

Prefer an orthogonal factorization to explicitly inverting the normal-equation matrix

---

### Why normal equations square the condition number {#derive-the-normal-equation-condition-number}

For full column rank, every $\sigma_j>0$ and
\begin{gather*}
\mat{A}^\top\mat{A}=\mat{V}\mat{\Sigma}^2\mat{V}^\top\\
\|\mat{A}\|_2=\sigma_1,\qquad\|\mat{A}^{\dagger}\|_2=1/\sigma_n\\
\kappa_2(\mat{A})=\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_n},\qquad
\kappa_2(\mat{A}^\top\mat{A})=\frac{\sigma_1^2}{\sigma_n^2}=\kappa_2(\mat{A})^2
\end{gather*}

The normal-equation matrix has eigenvalues $\sigma_j^2$

This explains a numerical cost of forming $\mat{A}^\top\mat{A}$ explicitly


## Practice separating fit from coefficients {#practice-separating-fit-from-coefficients}

<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>For the redundant-feature example, describe every least-squares solution<br>Verify that the residual is perpendicular to both columns<br>Explain why $[3/2,3/2]^\top$ has the smallest norm</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Solutions: $[3/2+t,3/2-t]^\top$, t real. Each column dotted with [-1,1]^T is zero. Squared coefficient norm is 9/2+2t^2, minimized at t=0.
:::

when time is short. No result in the SVD or regression sections depends on
this section or on the optional Special Topics deck.
:::

- [Sines and cosines form orthogonal directions](#sines-and-cosines-form-orthogonal-directions)
- [Complex inner products use conjugation](#complex-inner-products-use-conjugation)

## Approximate a function in a finite-dimensional subspace {#approximate-a-function-in-a-finite-dimensional-subspace}

Choose an orthonormal list $q_1,\ldots,q_n$ using the integral inner product
\begin{gather*}
p_n=\sum_{j=1}^n\langle q_j,f\rangle q_j\\
\|f-p_n\|^2=\|f\|^2-\sum_{j=1}^n|\langle q_j,f\rangle|^2
\end{gather*}

$p_n$ is the unique best approximation in their span

This is the same projection geometry used in regression

---

### Derive the projection error identity {#derive-the-function-projection-error}

Put $c_j=\langle q_j,f\rangle$ and $p_n=\sum_jc_jq_j$
\begin{gather*}
\langle q_i,f-p_n\rangle=c_i-\sum_jc_j\langle q_i,q_j\rangle=0\\
\|p_n\|^2=\sum_j|c_j|^2,\qquad
\|f\|^2=\|p_n\|^2+\|f-p_n\|^2\\
\|f-p_n\|^2=\|f\|^2-\sum_j|c_j|^2
\end{gather*}

For any other $g$ in the chosen span:
\begin{equation*}
\|f-g\|^2=\|f-p_n\|^2+\|p_n-g\|^2
\end{equation*}

Orthogonality proves both the error formula and unique best approximation


## Orthogonalize the first two polynomial directions {#orthogonalize-the-first-two-polynomial-directions}

On $[0,1]$, begin with $1$ and $t$
\begin{gather*}
q_1(t)=1,\qquad w_2(t)=t-\int_0^1t\,\dif t=t-1/2\\
\int_0^1(t-1/2)^2\,\dif t=1/12,\qquad
q_2(t)=\sqrt{12}(t-1/2)
\end{gather*}

Gram–Schmidt works on functions as well as coordinate vectors

::: {.notes}
This is the beginning of shifted, normalized Legendre polynomials. Higher-degree formulas are optional; retain the same interval and weight when using orthogonality.
:::

---

### Evaluate the polynomial normalization integral {#polynomial-normalization-arithmetic}

\begin{align*}
\langle 1,t\rangle&=\int_0^1t\,\dif t=[t^2/2]_0^1=1/2\\
\|t-1/2\|^2
&=\int_0^1(t^2-t+1/4)\,\dif t\\
&=[t^3/3-t^2/2+t/4]_0^1=\frac13-\frac12+\frac14=\frac1{12}\\
q_2(t)&=\frac{t-1/2}{\sqrt{1/12}}=\sqrt{12}(t-1/2)
\end{align*}

$\langle q_1,q_2\rangle=\sqrt{12}(1/2-1/2)=0$ and $\|q_2\|^2=12/12=1$


## A best linear approximation to a quadratic function {#a-best-linear-approximation-to-a-quadratic-function}

For $f(t)=t^2$ on $[0,1]$:
\begin{gather*}
\langle q_1,f\rangle=1/3,\qquad
\langle q_2,f\rangle=\sqrt{12}/12\\
p(t)=\frac13+\frac{\sqrt{12}}{12}\sqrt{12}(t-1/2)=t-1/6\\
\|f-p\|^2=\frac15-\frac19-\frac1{12}=\frac1{180}
\end{gather*}

Continuous least squares minimizes an integral of squared error

It need not interpolate either endpoint

---

### Integrate the coefficients and the squared error {#quadratic-function-projection-arithmetic}

\begin{align*}
\langle q_1,f\rangle&=\int_0^1t^2\,\dif t=1/3\\
\langle q_2,f\rangle&=\sqrt{12}\int_0^1(t^3-t^2/2)\,\dif t
=\sqrt{12}\left(\frac14-\frac16\right)=\frac{\sqrt{12}}{12}\\
\|f\|^2&=\int_0^1t^4\,\dif t=1/5\\
\|f-p\|^2&=\frac15-\left(\frac13\right)^2-\left(\frac{\sqrt{12}}{12}\right)^2
=\frac{36-20-15}{180}=\frac1{180}
\end{align*}

The error subtracts squared coefficients in an orthonormal basis


## Sines and cosines form orthogonal directions {#sines-and-cosines-form-orthogonal-directions}

On $[0,1]$, use $1$ and, for $k\ge1$:
\begin{equation*}
\sqrt2\cos(2\pi kt),\qquad \sqrt2\sin(2\pi kt)
\end{equation*}

These functions are orthonormal under $\int_0^1 f(t)g(t)\,\dif t$

Finite sums approximate a function by its periodic components

The constant coefficient is the mean $\int_0^1f(t)\,\dif t$

::: {.notes}
Use 1-periodic extension. Orthogonality follows from trigonometric product identities. Finite truncations are projections; do not assert pointwise convergence of every Fourier series. The infinite completeness statement is in the L2 sense.
:::

---

### Use product identities to check the Fourier normalization {#derive-real-fourier-orthogonality}

For each nonzero integer $h$:
$\int_0^1\cos(2\pi ht)\,\dif t=\int_0^1\sin(2\pi ht)\,\dif t=0$
\begin{align*}
2\cos(2\pi kt)\cos(2\pi\ell t)
&=\cos(2\pi(k-\ell)t)+\cos(2\pi(k+\ell)t)\\
2\sin(2\pi kt)\sin(2\pi\ell t)
&=\cos(2\pi(k-\ell)t)-\cos(2\pi(k+\ell)t)
\end{align*}

For $k,\ell\ge1$, integration gives zero when $k\ne\ell$, and $1/2$ when $k=\ell$

Sine–cosine products integrate to zero by the corresponding sine-sum identity

Multiplication by $\sqrt2$ changes squared norm $1/2$ to $1$


## Complex inner products use conjugation {#complex-inner-products-use-conjugation}

On $\mathbb{C}^n$, adopt $\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle=\vct{u}^*\vct{v}$

Conjugate linear in the first argument, linear in the second
\begin{gather*}
\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle=\overline{\langle\vct{v},\vct{u}\rangle},\qquad
\|\vct{v}\|^2=\sum_j|v_j|^2\\
\langle f,g\rangle=\int_0^1\overline{f(t)}g(t)\,\dif t
\end{gather*}

Ordinary real-angle formulas do not directly define a complex angle

::: {.notes}
Declare the argument convention explicitly; some books adopt the opposite one. With this convention coefficients in an orthonormal expansion are <q_j,v>, as in the real case. Orthogonality means the complex inner product is zero.
:::


## Complex exponentials package the Fourier pairs {#complex-exponentials-package-the-fourier-pairs}

For integers $k$, let $q_k(t)=e^{2\pi\sqrt{-1}\,kt}$
\begin{gather*}
\langle q_k,q_\ell\rangle
=\int_0^1e^{2\pi\sqrt{-1}(\ell-k)t}\,\dif t
=\begin{cases}1,&k=\ell\\0,&k\ne\ell\end{cases}\\
c_k=\langle q_k,f\rangle
=\int_0^1e^{-2\pi\sqrt{-1}\,kt}f(t)\,\dif t
\end{gather*}

For real $f$, $c_{-k}=\overline{c_k}$

[Fourier matrices and FFT]({{< meta decks.d11.file >}}#fourier-coordinates-and-the-fft) turn sampled versions into fast coordinate calculations

---

### Integrate a nonzero frequency difference {#derive-complex-fourier-orthogonality}

Write $\mathrm{i}=\sqrt{-1}$ and $h=\ell-k\in\mathbb{Z}$
\begin{equation*}
\int_0^1e^{2\pi\mathrm{i}ht}\,\dif t
=\begin{cases}
1,&h=0\\
\displaystyle\left[\frac{e^{2\pi\mathrm{i}ht}}{2\pi\mathrm{i}h}\right]_0^1
=\frac{e^{2\pi\mathrm{i}h}-1}{2\pi\mathrm{i}h}=0,&h\ne0
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}

For real $f$, conjugation passes through the integral:
\begin{equation*}
\overline{c_k}
=\overline{\int_0^1e^{-2\pi\mathrm{i}kt}f(t)\,\dif t}
=\int_0^1e^{2\pi\mathrm{i}kt}f(t)\,\dif t=c_{-k}
\end{equation*}


## Finite projections and infinite expansions have different meanings {#finite-projections-and-infinite-expansions-have-different-meanings}

An algebraic basis represents each vector with a [finite]{.alert} linear combination

A complete orthonormal Fourier system represents square-integrable functions by limits in the $L^2$ norm
\begin{equation*}
\left\|f-\sum_{k=-N}^{N}c_kq_k\right\|_{L^2}\longrightarrow0
\end{equation*}

Convergence in mean square does not automatically imply convergence at every point

::: {.notes}
Use L2 equivalence classes. A continuous function viewed as L2 has the same finite integral projections. At jump discontinuities, familiar piecewise smooth Fourier series converge to midpoint values; leave detailed pointwise theorems to a later course. The Fourier system is not an algebraic Hamel basis.
:::


## Practice extracting Fourier coordinates {#practice-extracting-fourier-coordinates}


::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>For $f(t)=2+3\cos(2\pi t)-\sin(4\pi t)$, find its mean<br>Find its coefficients in the normalized real Fourier system<br>Which complex frequencies can have nonzero coefficients?</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Mean 2. Normalized real coefficients: 2 for constant, 3/sqrt(2) for sqrt(2)cos(2pi t), -1/sqrt(2) for sqrt(2)sin(4pi t); others zero. Complex frequencies 0, ±1, ±2. Complex coefficients c_1=c_-1=3/2, c_2=i/2, c_-2=-i/2.
:::


# Big Ideas {#big-ideas data-state="goldborder"}

- [Inner products]{.alert} define length, distance, and perpendicularity
- [Orthogonal projection]{.alert} gives the unique closest vector in a finite-dimensional subspace
- [Gram–Schmidt]{.alert} produces orthonormal directions with the same span
- [QR]{.alert} records those directions and triangular coordinates
- [Least squares]{.alert} fits the column-space component of the data
- [SVD]{.alert} separates orthonormal directions from stretches for every matrix
- [Pseudoinverses]{.alert} select minimum-norm fits; small singular values reveal sensitivity
- [Fourier approximation]{.alert} projects onto oscillatory directions

# What Can We Do with Vectors and Matrices? {#course-recap}

\* Optional

- Solve $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ — $[\mat{A}\mid\vct{b}]\xrightarrow{\text{swap, scale, add}}\text{echelon form}$, then back-substitute or continue to RREF
- Classify — [augmented-column pivot]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#pivots-organize-elimination) $\implies$ none. Otherwise $\vct{x}=\vct{x}_p+\vct{z}$, $\vct{z}\in\operatorname{null}(\mat{A})$ (unique if no free variables)
- Invert by Gauss–Jordan — $[\mat{A}\mid\mat{I}]\longrightarrow[\mat{I}\mid\mat{A}^{-1}]$ for nonsingular $\mat{A}$
- Add, scale, multiply, transpose — $\alpha\vct{u}+\beta\vct{v}$, $\alpha\mat{A}+\beta\mat{B}$, $\mat{A}\mat{B}$, $\mat{A}^\top$
- Apply a map — $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\sum_j x_j\vct{A}_j$, with $(\mat{A}\vct{x})_i=\vct{a}_i^\top\vct{x}$
- Build maps from basis images — $\mat{A}=[T(\vct{e}_1)\ \cdots\ T(\vct{e}_n)]$ for rotations, reflections, stretches, projections
- Compose and undo — $(\mat{B}\mat{A})\vct{x}=\mat{B}(\mat{A}\vct{x})$, $(\mat{B}\mat{A})^{-1}=\mat{A}^{-1}\mat{B}^{-1}$
- Determinant — $\det(\mat{A})=(-1)^s\prod_i u_{ii}$ after $s$ swaps and elimination without row scaling
- Signed scale — $\det(\mat{A}\mat{B})=\det(\mat{A})\det(\mat{B})$, $\det(\mat{A})\ne0\iff\mat{A}$ invertible
- Local scale $\lvert\det(\mat{J})\rvert$, Wronskian $W(t)\ne0\implies$ independent functions

---

<h2>What Can We Do with Vectors and Matrices?</h2>

- Subspace test — $\vct{0}\in S$, $\alpha\vct{u}+\beta\vct{v}\in S$ for $\vct{u},\vct{v}\in S$
- Span — $\mat{A}\vct{c}=\vct{b}$ solvable · Independence — $\operatorname{null}(\mat{A})=\{\vct{0}\}$
- Basis — independent + spanning, $\dim V=\#\text{ basis vectors}$ for vectors, polynomials, functions, matrices
- Four spaces — original pivot columns, nonzero echelon rows, $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{0}$, $\mat{A}^\top\vct{y}=\vct{0}$
- Rank and compatibility — $\operatorname{rank}(\mat{A})+\operatorname{nullity}(\mat{A})=n$, $\vct{b}\in\operatorname{col}(\mat{A})\iff\vct{b}\perp\operatorname{null}(\mat{A}^\top)$
- Change coordinates — $[\vct{x}]_{\mathcal C}=\mat{P}_{\mathcal C}^{-1}\mat{P}_{\mathcal B}[\vct{x}]_{\mathcal B}$, map matrix $\mat{P}_{\mathcal C}^{-1}\mat{A}\mat{P}_{\mathcal B}$
- Eigenvalues and eigenspaces — $\det(\lambda\mat{I}-\mat{A})=0$, $\operatorname{null}(\mat{A}-\lambda\mat{I})$
- Diagonalize if $\sum_\lambda\dim\operatorname{null}(\mat{A}-\lambda\mat{I})=n$ over the chosen field
- Check the spectrum — $\operatorname{tr}(\mat{A})=\sum_j\lambda_j$, $\det(\mat{A})=\prod_j\lambda_j$, conjugate pairs for real $\mat{A}$
- Powers and functions — $f(\mat{A})=\mat{V}f(\mat{D})\mat{V}^{-1}$ in an eigenbasis, $\vct{x}_k=\mat{A}^k\vct{x}_0$, $\vct{x}(t)=e^{t\mat{A}}\vct{x}(0)$

---

<h2>What Can We Do with Vectors and Matrices?</h2>

- $\mat{A}=\mat{P}\mat{L}\mat{U}$ — $\mat{P}$ restores row order, $\mat{L}$ unit lower triangular, $\mat{U}$ upper triangular for square $\mat{A}$
- \* $\mat{A}=\mat{C}\mat{R}$ — $\mat{C}$ original pivot columns, $\mat{R}$ nonzero RREF rows
- $\mat{A}=\mat{V}\mat{D}\mat{V}^{-1}$ — $\mat{V}$ eigenbasis, $\mat{D}=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_j)$, $\mat{V}^{-1}=\mat{V}^\top$ for an orthonormal eigenbasis
- $\mat{A}=\mat{Q}\mat{R}$ — full column rank, $\mat{Q}^\top\mat{Q}=\mat{I}$, $\mat{R}$ upper triangular
- \* $\mat{A}=\mat{U}_r\mat{\Sigma}_r\mat{V}_r^\top$ — SVD, orthonormal columns in $\mat{U}_r,\mat{V}_r$, positive diagonal $\mat{\Sigma}_r$
- Inner products — $\vct{u}^\top\vct{v}$, $\vct{u}^\top\mat{W}\vct{v}$ ($\mat{W}\succ0$), $\int fg$
- Length, distance, angle — $\|\vct{u}\|^2=\langle\vct{u},\vct{u}\rangle$, $\|\vct{u}-\vct{v}\|$, $\cos\theta=\langle\vct{u},\vct{v}\rangle/(\|\vct{u}\|\|\vct{v}\|)$
- Cross and triple products — $\vct{u}\times\vct{v}$ normal, $\|\vct{u}\times\vct{v}\|$ area, $\vct{w}^\top(\vct{u}\times\vct{v})$ signed volume
- Gram–Schmidt and projection — orthonormal columns in $\mat{Q}$, $\vct{p}=\mat{Q}\mat{Q}^\top\vct{b}$
- [Least squares](#fit-a-line-to-three-observations) — $\mat{A}^\top(\vct{b}-\mat{A}\widehat{\vct{x}})=\vct{0}$, solve $\mat{R}\widehat{\vct{x}}=\mat{Q}^\top\vct{b}$ using reduced QR

---

<h2>What Can We Do with Vectors and Matrices?</h2>

- PCA — covariance eigenvectors, variance along direction $j$ given by $\lambda_j$
- Matrix series — $\sum_{k=0}^\infty\mat{A}^k=(\mat{I}-\mat{A})^{-1}$ if every $|\lambda_j|<1$
- \* Frames, infinite bases, abstract kernels and ranges, generalized eigenvector chains
- \* Weighted least squares — $\min_{\vct{x}}\|\mat{W}^{1/2}(\mat{A}\vct{x}-\vct{b})\|^2$
- \* SVD tools — rank-$k$ truncation, $\widehat{\vct{x}}=\mat{A}^+\vct{b}$ (minimum norm), $\kappa(\mat{A})=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}$ (full column rank), ridge
- \* Function approximation — complex inner products, Fourier coefficients $c_k=\langle q_k,f\rangle$
- \* Principal axes and tensors — $\vct{x}^\top\mat{A}\vct{x}=\sum_j\lambda_j y_j^2$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis, product bases $\vct{u}_i\otimes\vct{v}_j$
- \* Signals and networks — DFT/FFT, convolution, power iteration, PageRank, graph Laplacians, left-null compatibility
